title: Ragtime versus jazz, and the society bands he knew
summary: He distinguishes ragtime from jazz, lists Oliver, Piron, Robichaux and their players, the origins of white bands, and recalls a slave pianist called Snowball.

story.theme_name: Dance halls, lake camps and riverboat bandstands
story.community_name: Dance halls, lake resorts and where bands played

blocks.x: A form of jazz music that you were playing? It was definitely not ragtime, I can tell you that. It was my interpretation of the difference between jazz and ragtime is, if you'll put it as simply as possible, is one is jerkier than the other one. And let's say the same difference that there is between jazz and swing, there is between ragtime and jazz. It was a smoother type of the same sort of music. But then our interest in the music became very deeper, much deeper personally, not with any idea of analysis. I wasn't... We didn't know anything about style. We didn't know anything about the various musicians, except we knew them by their names. And we danced enough by them to... them to know us. We knew Oliver. We knew Ori, Dodds, Johnny and Baby Dodds, Clarence Williams, A.J. Pierron was a great, great, had a great band. And for many years, they were the top society band. And then Robichaud did a great deal of the society stuff too. He also played at Louisiana, which is now Diamond Jim Moran's place, but it was a magnificent, well-run restaurant in those days and they had wonderful parties. But when was this? That was from 1914 up to the outbreak of World War I. And then after the war, it resumed again. Those bands were all readers. They were not... They were wonderful musicians. We had Lorenzo Teo on clarinet, who still goes down in history, one of the greatest clarinets. He was with Pierron. And Pierron also had a fellow by the name of Steve Lewis on piano, who was, I think, the model from which Fats Waller got so, you know, most of his great stuff. And then there was a drummer by the name of Louis Cottrell, who is credited with being the first drummer who introduced the press role into the music. But these people were playing society music and they couldn't really blow that top in real rat-gut barrel-house jazz. Now, Robichaud, who was this left-hand... Both Negro bands, light Negro, was a left-hand violinist, and he had a society orchestra too. But he always included a hot... One hot man in it who'd take off on choruses. But the straight reader would predominate all the way through and they had fine rhythm. Then the real origins of the early white New Orleans bands, the bands that people know as the original Dixieland Jazz Band, the New Orleans Rhythm Kings, didn't exist at all, in fact, in New Orleans, until they went away from here and started recording them. They had to make up a name and they assumed those names. But I knew all those men individually and the bands were continually changing, interchanging musicians and personalities. And in that way we were about their age, maybe they were a few years older, but we would sit there and listen very much. Then we'd go home and try to play the same thing on string instruments. The attitude of the older folks, I remember my father saying that when he was a young buck around 18, they had one of the slaves that was called Snowball. He was as black as the Ace of Spades, who always was brought in to play piano, totally uninstructed, but he said he played ten-fingered piano that they danced to, the Schottish and the Maezurka and all those old-time dances. He said he was magnificent. The attitude, of course, was that he was an entertainer and there because he was a fine musician and had good rhythm. But there wasn't any idea of a leveling process through the music or a consideration on anything but a hired person that they paid for. Even the slaves got it or paid if they did something special like that. I can't go on without another question of some kind.
